title: Preface
summary: Front matter of the NRO Center for the Study of National Reconnaissance publication 'The Dorian Files Revealed: A Compendium of the NRO's Manned Orbiting Laboratory Documents,' edited by James D. Outzen, Ph.D., August 2015. It includes Carl Berger's 'A History of the Manned Orbiting Laboratory Program Office.' It describes the CSNR's mission (research on national reconnaissance history and analysis), copyright and contact details, how to obtain copies via GPO or CSNR, and publication info (Chantilly, Virginia; ISBN 978-1-937219-18-5).

title: Center for the Study of national reConnaiSSanCe

nodes.title: Center for the Study of national reConnaiSSanCe (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes the NRO's Center for the Study of National Reconnaissance (CSNR), an independent research body that studies national reconnaissance through social science and history to inform NRO leadership, with copyright, contact, and ordering information and publication details. Presents the table of contents of Carl Berger's history of the Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL) program Office, covering its origins in early space station planning, the Dyna-Soar and Gemini context, the MOL approval in 1965, program organization, the manned/unmanned debates, budget and schedule problems, congressional and range controversies, NASA coordination, termination in 1969, and post-mortem analysis of costs, hardware, and whether it could have been saved.

nodes.title: Foreword
nodes.summary: Foreword by Robert A. McDonald, NRO Center for the Study of National Reconnaissance, introducing The Dorian Files Revealed, a compendium of secret Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL) documents. It notes the program's public history, its previously hidden role as a reconnaissance platform, and themes including public affairs, US Air Force/NASA/NRO coordination, manned space station origins, budget competition, and program termination. It also cites MOL's legacy and the value of the collection for historians.

nodes.title: Preface
nodes.summary: Preface to the third CSNR compendium of declassified Dorian Files, about 20,000 pages on the Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL) reconnaissance program. It introduces Carl Berger's MOL administrative history, with redactions bracketed, a documents index on DVD, a planned 2016 crew history, and thanks to NRO staff, the Air Force museum, crew members, and CSNR personnel.

nodes.title: Manned Orbiting Laboratory and Early U.S. Space Reconnaissance
key_items: limitationS of early SpaCe reConnaiSS anCe ColleCtion
nodes.summary: Covers Johnson's 1965 Manned Orbiting Laboratory announcement, then early US reconnaissance origins: post-WWII aircraft overflights, U-2 and SR-71 limits, Rand's 1946 space concept, and Samos, Corona, Gambit and GRAB/Poppy satellites. Describes intelligence gains on Soviet weapons, then limitations: cloud-obscured imagery, slow retargeting, malfunctions, and no on-orbit repairs.

summary: Describes the NRO's Center for the Study of National Reconnaissance (CSNR), an independent research body applying social science and history to national reconnaissance, with publication details. Covers Carl Berger's history of the Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL): early space station planning, Dyna-Soar and Gemini context, 1965 approval, organization, manned/unmanned debates, budget and schedule problems, congressional and range disputes, NASA coordination, 1969 termination, and cost and salvage analysis. Foreword and preface introduce the declassified Dorian Files (about 20,000 pages), with a documents index and planned crew history. Early US reconnaissance origins are also covered: overflights, U-2 and SR-71 limits, Rand's 1946 concept, Samos, Corona, Gambit, and GRAB/Poppy satellites, and their imagery limitations.

title: Origins and Limits of US National Space Reconnaissance
key_items: limitationS of early SpaCe reConnaiSSanCe ColleCtion
summary: Introduces President Johnson's 1965 Manned Orbiting Laboratory for manned space reconnaissance. Covers early US aerial reconnaissance (U-2, A-12, SR-71) and its obsolescence after the 1960 Powers shootdown. Traces RAND's 1946 advocacy of space intelligence, the Samos program, and the CIA's Corona satellites, which succeeded in August 1960, plus the GRAB signals satellite. Describes Corona and Gambit imagery, Grab and Poppy signals intelligence, and their Cold War value. Notes limitations: cloud-obscured imagery, slow retargeting, and malfunctions that could not be repaired on orbit.

title: The Dorian Program: MOL Reconnaissance Mission and Intra-Government Cooperation
summary: Describes the Air Force's Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL) program, announced in 1963 as a crewed space platform and replacing the cancelled X-20 Dynasoar. It reveals the secret Dorian compartment, which planned imagery and signals intelligence using a Kodak camera with improved resolution, spotting scope targeting, and crew repair. It explains the reliance on NASA Gemini capsules and NRO sensors, and the technical challenges of 60-day missions.

title: mol program ChallengeS
summary: An introduction by James D. Outzen to the Dorian Files compendium on the Air Force's Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL), announced in 1963 as a crewed station. Secretly, MOL's Dorian project aimed at manned imagery and signals reconnaissance, with a Kodak camera offering better resolution and crew repair. It relied on NASA Gemini capsules and NRO sensors. Challenges included long-duration missions, Vietnam War budget pressures, and rivalry with Hexagon; MOL was terminated in 1969. Its legacy includes astronauts, advances in space suits, modular station design, segmented mirrors, and the Dorian camera's influence on Hexagon.

title: the mol program legaCy
summary: Describes the Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL) program: its Vietnam War-era budget delays, its termination in June 1969 after Hexagon and Gambit-3 made it seem unnecessary, and its legacy. Legacy includes MOL-trained crew who became NASA astronauts and leaders, contributions to the Dorian camera, unmanned film-return designs, segmented mirror technology, flexible spacesuits, and linked multi-module concepts informing the ISS. Written by James D. Outzen of the NRO history center.

title: early Space Station planning
summary: Describes Hermann Oberth's 1923 proposal of orbital space stations with telescopes for observing Earth, and his mirror concepts for illumination or warfare. Covers the German V-2 team including Wernher von Braun, their 1944 arrest, postwar capture by US forces, and Arnold's 1945 report on space ships. Also covers their work at Fort Bliss and White Sands, 1950 public talk by von Braun on space stations, and Oberth's 1956 book on space telescopes for Earth observation.

title: the air forCe initiateS SpaCe Station planning
summary: Describes early USAF space station planning from 1957-1959: WADC studies of military satellites and manned stations, the 1957 Soviet satellite launches prompting US initiatives, contractor proposals (including a four-man station using Atlas ICBMs), the January 1958 USAF proposals (Manned Strategic Station, ARDC space laboratory task, ARPA's Suzanno study), General Boushey's 1958 testimony on orbital reconnaissance resolution and the role of human operators, LeMay's push to get a man into space, creation of NASA in July 1958 with transfer of Air Force space projects, and a 1959 SAB proposal for a permanently manned satellite command post.

title: the military orBital development SyStem
summary: Describes the Air Force's early space station planning in 1959-1962. In 1959 the USAF Director of Development Planning drafted a long-range space plan that first used the term 'manned orbital laboratory.' ARDC then solicited military test space station (MTSS) ideas, and five contractors studied designs in 1960-61. ASD proposed a 30-day station, and an MTSS conference in September 1961 noted gaps in zero-G and rendezvous knowledge. Subsequent steps covered OSD funding rejection, McNamara's approval of Dyna-Soar and a space laboratory, the MODS proposal (Program 287), the Five-Year Space Program, and its roughly $10 billion cost.

title: modS, Blue gemini, and the fiveyear SpaCe program
summary: Covers early 1962-63 USAF space station planning: Dr. Kavanau endorsed Phase I and the MODS (Military Orbital Development System) proposal; the PCP was approved July 1962, then revised after McMillan judged $14.7M too high. The Ferguson task force's Five-Year Space Program (over $10B FY63-67) was endorsed by a SAB subcommittee and forwarded to OSD. Zuckert limited requests to Midas, Saint, MODS, and Blue Gemini ($363M FY64), citing MODS advantages and Blue Gemini as a MODS stepping stone. OSD rejected the plan over cost and duplication with NASA Gemini, and Blue Gemini's six-flight plan is described.

title: the naSa-dod gemini agreement
summary: The text covers Air Force efforts in 1962-1963 to pursue military manned space programs. It describes the Air Force's FY1964 budget recommendations (Midas, Saint, MODS, Blue Gemini, costing $363M), the Blue Gemini flight plan, and OSD's rejection of them over cost and duplication with NASA. It then explains the January 1963 NASA-DoD Gemini agreement creating the Gemini Program Planning Board, its recommended military experiments (~$16.1M), and McNamara's directives. Finally, it covers the NASA-DoD dispute over a NASA space station study and the restrictions in prior agreements. Endnotes list the sources cited.

title: a n ational Space Station
summary: Covers 1963 DoD-NASA tensions over a NASA space station study: OSD invoked the 1961/January 1963 agreements requiring mutual consent for new manned programs after Dryden's March 4 testimony on fiscal 1964 study contracts for a manned orbiting laboratory. USAF (Ritland, Zuckert) objected, McNamara and Webb compromised on joint sponsorship and mutual consent for hardware. Air Force then proposed a national space station under DoD; McNamara supported it but urged caution. AACB planning and informal USAF-NASA data exchange, coordination of pre-program studies, and a NASA focal point were established.

title: air forCe propoSeS a n ational SpaCe Station
summary: Covers 1963 DoD-NASA disagreement over space station studies and their joint sponsorship and mutual-consent hardware rule; the Air Force's proposal for a national space station (MODS concept) assigned to DoD; McNamara's May 1963 request for a Manned Orbital Test Station Planning Group; AACB Manned Space Flight Panel coordination and formal information exchange (data, RFPs, proposals, observers); Heaton's proposal for parallel pre-program studies; Yarymovych as NASA focal point; July 1963 press coverage of MODS and MORL; and McNamara's and Webb's August 1963 letters to Vice President Johnson on military uses, surveillance, and the Manned Orbital Laboratory.

title: mcn amara’S report to viCe preSident JohnSon
summary: Covers 1963 NASA-DoD coordination on a national/manned orbital space station. The AACB Manned Space Flight Panel urged more formal information exchange. Vice President Johnson asked McNamara and Webb for views on space station uses; McNamara cited laboratory, surveillance, and possible military roles and a need for a new national mission. Webb described the MOL project and proposed joint management recommendations. McNamara drafted a formal agreement; NASA proposed an alternative, which McNamara signed 16 September 1963 with reservations about premature NASA MORL design spending. Study funding and approvals are noted.

title: a n ew naSa-dod SpaCe Station agreement
summary: Describes Cold War-era NASA-DoD coordination on a manned orbital space station. Covers Air Force Manned Orbital Laboratory (MOL) proposals, a McNamara-Webb agreement (Aug-Sept 1963) on joint studies, the NOSS pre-program study, NASA's MORL study cut from $3.5M to $1.2M to allow later DoD merger, and the Air Force's new Deputy Director of Development Planning office overseeing space station data exchange.

title: the air forCe oSS Study
summary: Describes Air Force efforts in 1963 to revive a military space station study after NASA's space station activities. Covers the proposed three-month Phase Zero MODS study, requests for Army and Navy mission input, the renaming to Orbital Space Station (OSS), funding requests and milestones, Deputy Secretary Gilpatric's review, Dr. Brown's reconnaissance-focused guidance, Dr. Flax's approval and RFPs sent to 45 firms, and OSD's limited funding approval. Ends with a note that contract award was delayed by late-1963 decisions, followed by endnotes citing supporting memos and letters.

title: dyna-Soar Killed, mol approved

nodes.title: the dyna-Soar/gemini review
nodes.summary: Covers the 1963 review of Air Force Dyna-Soar (X-20) versus NASA's Gemini. McNamara, doubtful of Dyna-Soar, asked DDR&E to review it; the Air Force defended it as vital, and NASA supported its technology value. Deputy DDR&E Rubel questioned its importance and listed options including cancellation. McNamara's on-site review and four military space missions were addressed; McMillan admitted neither system yet offered significant military capability. By fall 1963 McNamara favored terminating Dyna-Soar in favor of Gemini plus a DoD space station. Brown analyzed six station configurations (costs $470-$1,286 million), preferring a Titan III-launched four-man station costing $983 million, with an improved ferry vehicle and ASSET testing, and recommended cancelling X-20 and transferring Gemini to the Air Force. Footnotes cover Soviet manned flights and the ASSET test.

nodes.title: Brown reCommendS a defenSe SpaCe Station and naSa maKeS a Counter-propoSal
nodes.summary: Covers the 1963 termination of the Air Force's Dyna-Soar (X-20) program. McNamara asked for review of USAF space projects for four missions (satellite inspection/destruction, satellite protection, reconnaissance, orbital weapons); McMillan admitted X-20 and Gemini lacked military on-orbit capability. Brown proposed a DoD space station (six configurations, $709.5M-$1,286M; preferred Titan III four-room station at $983M) and cancelling X-20. NASA counter-proposed a simpler Gemini/Titan III orbiting laboratory ($593M). On 30 November McNamara agreed to build a military space station using NASA's approach.

nodes.title: the air forCe’S laSt effort to Save dyna-Soar
nodes.summary: Describes the Air Force's last-ditch effort in late 1963 to save the X-20 Dyna-Soar: a Headquarters USAF paper proposing X-20 use for a space station, Gen. Hester's and Secretary Zuckert's objections to cancellation, and Dr. Flax's cost critiques of Gemini recovery and Alternative 3. It covers OSD's 5 December decision to cancel X-20 in favor of a Manned Orbital Program, and McNamara's 10 December announcement of MOL as an experimental, Air Force-managed two-man orbital lab.

nodes.title: announCement of the mol proJ eCt
nodes.summary: Covers the cancellation of Dyna-Soar and the approval of the Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL). A technical team disputed Alternative 3's cost ($1.5B vs $983.0M; Flax estimated $1.9B). Gilpatric directed a Manned Orbital Program replacing X-20 and augmenting ASSET. McNamara announced MOL on 10 December 1963 as an experimental Air Force-managed program saving $100M. The DoD-NASA agreement of 27 December 1963 (Hall and Mueller) set roles, Gemini B/MOL hardware, Titan III booster, a Coordinating Board, ASSET augmentation, and future space station studies. A January 1964 contract authorization for McDonnell is also noted.

nodes.title: the dod-naSa mol agreement
nodes.summary: Covers the 1963-64 DoD-NASA agreements on the Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL) and Gemini B. Key points: a 27 Dec 1963 Hall-Mueller joint paper on military and NASA manned orbital requirements, rejecting an operational 'space station' aim and noting possible future large-station needs; a 10-point summary of agreements (USAF-managed MOL, Gemini modified as passenger vehicle, Titan III booster, X-20 cancelled, ASSET augmented, a Coordinating Board); and a late-Jan 1964 contract authorization. Includes endnote citations.

summary: Covers the 1963 termination of Air Force Dyna-Soar (X-20) in favor of NASA's Gemini and a DoD space station. McNamara ordered reviews; Brown's six station configurations ($470M-$1,286M) preferred a $983M Titan III four-man station; NASA countered with a $593M Gemini/Titan III lab. The Air Force's last effort to save X-20 failed; OSD cancelled it 5 December. McNamara announced the Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL) on 10 December 1963, and a 27 December DoD-NASA agreement set roles, hardware, a Coordinating Board, ASSET augmentation, and MOL/Gemini B terms. A January 1964 contract authorization followed.

title: planning the m anned orbiting laboratory

nodes.title: planning the m anned orbiting laboratory (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes the Air Force's planning of the Manned Military Orbiting Laboratory (MMOL, later renamed MOL) from December 1963 to June 1964, following Dr. Brown's 11 December program guidance. The guidance states the purpose is to assess the military utility of man in space, with equipment chosen to support and challenge the astronaut's flexibility and judgment. Envisioned activities include scientific observation of space and earth, equipment adjustment and repair, and tests of coping with unusual situations, with provision for crew comfort (rest, exercise, freedom from spacesuits). Proposed missions include reconnaissance with camera equipment for threat warning, responding to simulated enemy-target requests by locating, photographing, processing and transmitting data, optical viewers for real-time target search, and infrared tests to assess human interpretation of signals from missiles, ships and ground sites. Other guidance covers use of NASA's Houston control facilities and tracking network, procurement of Gemini B capsules (via NASA if changes are minor, directly with McDonnell if major), funding of $10 million for FY1964 and $75 million for FY1965, a development plan due to OSD by year's end, and a call for DDR&E-level management control similar to the Titan III arrangement.

nodes.title: the air forCe reSponSe
nodes.summary: Covers the Air Force's response to the MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) program guidelines, December 1963 to March 1964. Schriever directed SSD to prepare a development plan (six launches, first manned flight late 1967) and an ASSET plan. General Bleymaier's task force proposed a reconnaissance-focused plan, which the Air Staff Board and Secretary Zuckert reviewed, raising launch schedule and mission concerns. Dr. Hall criticized the plan and urged earlier launches. Dr. McMillan, NRO Director, pushed for approved objectives over reconnaissance, leading to unified experiment planning. Funding, OSS studies, and DDR&E oversight were addressed. Aerospace and advisory groups favored surveillance; Project Forecast also backed manned reconnaissance. McMillan and Schriever agreed on overt pointing experiments, while NRO's covert DORIAN studies and BYEMAN security were established.

nodes.title: poliCy for the ConduCt of the mol program
nodes.summary: Describes MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) program policy from March 1964: experiments are primary objectives, with orbital tests only after ground and aircraft testing. Covers Dr. McMillan's directives, Dr. Brown's view that experiments must be specified so man can show advantages over machines, and the PTDP submitted to AFSC on 1 April 1964. The MOL Experiments Working Group reviewed over 400 proposals, reduced them to 59, then to 12 primary and 18 secondary experiments (P-1 to P-12 listed, including acquisition and tracking, direct viewing, electromagnetic detection, maintenance, EVA, navigation, biomedical evaluation; P-13 to P-15 added later). Covers schedule (unmanned launch June 1968, manned 1969), cost of $5.5 million, and the Dr. Flax D&F authorizing OSS study contracts on 13 April 1964.

nodes.title: mol pre-phaSe i go-ahead iS approved
nodes.summary: Chapter IV of a history of the NRO's Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL), covering Dec 1963 to June 1964. It describes Air Force and OSD approval of MOL pre-Phase I studies: Dr. Flax's April 1964 request, a $6 million funding plan for experiment and support studies, and McNamara's authorization with conditions (delayed Apollo/Gemini contracts, deletion of experiment P-9, emphasis on ground simulation). It details the spring-summer 1964 contract awards to about 13 contractors totaling roughly $3.2 million, the McMillan-Shriever exchange on simulation and objectives, and the revised development plan. Endnotes list the sources cited.

summary: Air Force planning of the Manned Military Orbiting Laboratory (MMOL, later MOL), Dec 1963 to June 1964: Brown's program guidance on assessing military utility of man in space, experiments, reconnaissance missions, funding, and Gemini B procurement. Covers the Air Force response (development plan, task force, Zuckert and Hall reviews, McMillan and Schriever agreement on overt experiments and NRO covert studies), MOL policy (experiments as primary objectives, 59 then 12 primary and 18 secondary experiments, schedule, cost, OSS studies), and Pre-Phase I approval (funding, McNamara's conditions, about 13 contract awards).

title: evolution of the mol management Structure
summary: Chapter V traces the evolution of the MOL (Manned Orbital Laboratory) management structure. In 1963, USAF sought executive management of a national space station, leading to the Deputy Director of Development Planning, Space office under Col. Kenneth Schultz, which coordinated with NASA. After McNamara killed Dyna-Soar and started MOL in December 1963, AFSC proposed a Pentagon-level MOL Special Program Office under Gen. Schriever, which the Air Staff and Under Secretary McMillan initially considered but then rejected. Field organization followed: an SSD Deputy Commander for Manned Space Systems under Gen. Bleymaier, with a Navy field office added. In April 1964 McMillan called for a MOL office directly responsive to the Secretary and Chief of Staff, leading to the June 1964 redesignation as Assistant for the MOL Program, an interim arrangement discussed further in Chapter VII.

title: endnoteS
summary: Endnotes listing 1963-1964 Air Force documents on the Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL) program and the National Space Station Program. They cover letters and memos among McKee, Ferguson, McMillan, Schriever, Ritland and Funk on DoD/NASA agreement implementation, AFSC draft proposals, field-level MOL management, and the MOL Coordination Office. Also includes some garbled OCR fragments.

title: reSultS of the pre-phaSe i inveStigation S
key_items: dod/naSa “dupliCation, “CongreSSional CritiCiSm and the Budget ConferenCe of 7-8 deCemBer 1964
summary: AFSC's 1964 MOL schedule (first unmanned launch 1968, manned 1969) was criticized by OSD and Air Staff, prompting Bleymaier's alternative schedules (experimental flights 18 months after go-ahead, manned-capable within 24-32 months) and a September 1964 Brady briefing promising a 2-man lab by mid-1967. Delays from OSD (Brown) stalled the RFP release and synopsis, frustrating USAF. NASA's competing Apollo-based space station studies (Apollo X) led McNamara to propose a DoD-NASA consolidation, which Webb rejected. Senator Anderson urged merging the programs. The 7-8 December 1964 budget conference approved MOL with $150M for FY1966, prioritized military observation technology and manned assembly, and set a review for May 1965. Pre-Phase I 'black' simulations (Eastman Kodak, Lockheed) and 'white' contractor studies, plus IDA reviews, supported MOL's feasibility for man-in-the-loop tracking, maintenance, navigation, and life support. Endnotes cite the sources.

title: the laBoratory vehiCle deSign Competition

nodes.title: the laBoratory vehiCle deSign Competition (intro)
nodes.summary: Covers early 1965 MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) program changes: Dr. Brown's 4 January 1965 directive redirecting studies toward military observation and in-orbit assembly, possible use of NASA Apollo as alternative to Titan IIIC/Gemini B, and three industry preliminary design contracts. McMillan implemented it on 8 January, and Greer was tasked with black payload studies. Also covers NRO security concerns over implied reconnaissance mission, the Project DORIAN separation of reconnaissance from non-reconnaissance work, and the 5 February security procedures. Finally, it notes the management structure dispute, where Schriever wanted a single central MOL office and McMillan kept the Air Staff office.

nodes.title: worrieS over mol SeCurity
nodes.summary: Covers the Dorian/MOL security dispute of January 1965: Dr. Brown's 4 January memo on a MOL reconnaissance capability was judged a security violation by General Martin, who urged prompt decisions. A working group proposed separating reconnaissance tasks (DORIAN/BYEMAN) from non-reconnaissance MOL work; General Greer endorsed it, and Dr. McMillan approved it on 5 February with special security procedures. Also describes a revised MOL management structure: Schriever pushed for a single integrated office, and McMillan met with staff in September 1964 to address it.

nodes.title: a reviSed mol management StruCture
nodes.summary: The text covers early 1965 security and management developments in the MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) program. After Dr. Brown's January 4 memorandum, General Martin warned that it implied a reconnaissance mission and violated NRO security, prompting a working group and Project DORIAN/BYEMAN separation of reconnaissance work from non-reconnaissance work, approved by McMillan in February. The text then describes the revised MOL management structure: a Policy Committee, General Evans as Special Assistant and Assistant Deputy Commander for Space, Air Force Space Panel concerns about Air Staff participation, and early-1965 discussions with NASA about using Apollo for MOL.

nodes.title: naSa’S mol/apollo Study
nodes.summary: Covers MOL management structure in early 1965 (MOL Policy Committee, Special Assistant, AFSC roles, Directorate of Special Projects) and McMillan/Brown's January 1965 requests to NASA for Apollo support in a DoD MOL study. NASA designated Garbarini as counterpart, formed a DoD/NASA ad hoc study group, and exchanged data, but USAF withheld P-15 details under DORIAN/BYEMAN security, leading NASA's MOL-Apollo team to flawed conclusions. Schedule and cost problems for Saturn/Apollo are noted, with NASA's May 1965 report claiming it could meet MOL requirements. McNamara's January 1965 announcements, the Webb joint statement, and his letter to Humphrey on the MOL decision options, including Gemini use, are also described.

nodes.title: approaChing a mol deCiSion
nodes.summary: Chapter VII of the Dorian Files covers January–June 1965 developments in the MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) program. It describes NASA's Saturn/Apollo alternative versus Titan IIIC/Gemini B, McNamara's three-option decision framing, and the AFSC request for proposals, with four contractors (Boeing, Douglas, GE, Lockheed) selected for 60-day studies. It also covers covert DORIAN optical reconnaissance studies, funding, McMillan's guidance prioritizing high-resolution optics, the source selection ranking, top-level briefings, and Congressional support after Leonov's spacewalk. Endnotes list sources.

summary: Covers early-1965 MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) changes: Brown's January directive toward military observation and in-orbit assembly, NASA Apollo as an alternative, and industry study contracts. Security concerns over implied reconnaissance led to separating DORIAN/BYEMAN reconnaissance work. Management structure disputes, the revised management structure, and NASA's MOL/Apollo study and data-withholding problems are described. McNamara's decision options, the four-contractor 60-day studies, optical reconnaissance funding, source selection, and Congressional support are also covered.

title: the mol program deCi Sion 25 august 1965

nodes.title: the air forCe propoSal
nodes.summary: Describes the Air Force's 28 June 1965 proposal to OSD for a Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL): a Titan IIIC/Gemini B six-vehicle program (one unmanned, five manned, first flight late 1968, last early 1970) costing $1,653 million. It targets optical reconnaissance at one-foot resolution using a 60-inch aperture, with a larger-aperture alternative. It argues the program is faster and more certain than unmanned systems, citing the Cuban missile crisis need for credible imagery. A second paper covered management, the two-contractor choice (Douglas and General Electric), NRO relations, and security policy.

nodes.title: dr. h ornig approveS, with qualifiCationS
nodes.summary: Covers Dr. Hornig's 30 June 1965 evaluation endorsing MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) approval with qualifications: he accepts the Air Force's finding that manned systems outperform unmanned ones on resolution, but flags untested mirror technology, pattern recognition and pointing problems that could narrow the gap, unproven manned performance, and political risks (privacy or overflight objections, USSR perception of MOL as a weapons system). He recommends developing unmanned subsystems in parallel and high-level political oversight of public disclosure and contingencies. Also covers Budget Director Schultze's 8 July 1965 doubts about the $1 billion extra development and $200 million annual cost versus GAMBIT-3 unmanned alternatives.

nodes.title: the Budget Bureau expreSSeS douBt
nodes.summary: Chapter VIII on the MOL program decision (Aug 1965). Hornig warned of serious political risks: manned surveillance could be seen as overflight or as a space weapons system, so high-level oversight of public disclosure and contingency plans was advised, though manned orbital activity had become routinely accepted. The Budget Bureau's Schultze questioned MOL's superiority over unmanned systems like GAMBIT-3, given about $1.6B extra cost, and opposed proceeding without clear need. After DoD studies lowered the cost gap to about $300-400M, he withdrew objections, on condition of reappraisal if the gap grew substantially within six months.

nodes.title: State department and Cia viewS
nodes.summary: On 9 July 1965 the Space Council reviewed the McNamara memo on MOL security, information handling, and a proposed public announcement, identifying tasks before any announcement, including coordination with State. Brown forwarded the memo and an information-controls policy paper to State. On 16 August, Secretary Rusk said he had no objection to proceeding if justified for national defense, urged tight control and careful publicity emphasizing MOL's experimental nature, and advised avoiding any suggestion of an operational capability. CIA Director Raborn cautiously endorsed MOL, weighing photographic resolution against cost, time, and intelligence value.

nodes.title: mCnamara reCommendS mol program approval
nodes.summary: McNamara recommends President approve MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) program on 24 Aug 1965, releasing $150M and starting contract definition in FY1966. Goals: semi-operational use by late 1968 with sub-foot resolution photography, high-resolution optical technology for manned or unmanned use, a facility for other military applications (SIGINT, radar, ocean surveillance), and experiments on human assembly of large space structures. Program runs under NRO security with low-key public information. Concurrences came from Rusk, Raborn, Hornig, Webb, and Humphrey; BoB withdrew objection pending cost reappraisal. Justified by Cuban crisis reconnaissance needs. An unmanned version will be pursued in parallel, with the manned version expected to offer better utility and to aid unmanned development.

nodes.title: the preSident’S deCiSion and puBliC reaCtion
nodes.summary: Describes the 1965 decision to proceed with the Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL), made after NASA's successful Gemini flights (Gemini 3, White's spacewalk, Gemini 5's record endurance and military experiments). President Johnson announced the program on 25 August 1965 with a Titan 3C booster and modified Gemini capsule, pledging peaceful intent. Press reaction was critical: The New York Times and Washington Post expressed concern over arms race and Air Force secrecy; about 45 citizens and several Congressmen objected; The New Republic saw potential stabilizing value. The Soviet Union, via Tass, Gen. Tolubko, and Izvestia, condemned MOL as espionage and combat-oriented. The State Department issued an airgram, and an interagency meeting discussed countering criticism, leading Dr. Welsh to publicly reaffirm MOL as non-weapons. Endnotes cite sources.

summary: Covers the August 1965 Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL) decision. The Air Force proposed a $1,653M Titan IIIC/Gemini B program for optical reconnaissance. Hornig endorsed it with qualifications on technology risk and political exposure. Budget Bureau doubts were withdrawn once the cost gap narrowed. State and CIA views were mixed, and McNamara recommended approval with $150M released. Johnson announced it on 25 August 1965 amid critical press and Soviet condemnation.

title: organizing for ContraCt definition

nodes.title: the n ew mol StruCture: two management ChannelS
nodes.summary: Covers USAF organization of MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) contract definition in 1965. Disputes between Generals Schriever and Martin over managing 'black' (reconnaissance) and 'white' contracts led to a plan with two management channels, approved by McNamara. Describes the roles of the Deputy Director, MOL (Berg), the Sensor Payload Office under Martin, and the Vice Director (Evans). Also covers leadership changes (McMillan replaced by Flax at NRO; Brown succeeding Zuckert; Foster at DDR&E), the DDR&E focal-point proposal, and procedures for funding and direction of NRO aspects of MOL.

nodes.title: proCedureS for guidanCe and direCtion of nro aSpeCtS of mol
nodes.summary: Covers post-1965 leadership changes: McMillan left the NRO, Flax succeeded him, Brown became Air Force Secretary, and Foster became DDR&E. It details the dispute over MOL management above the Air Force level, DDR&E's designation as MOL focal point (Fink as advisor), and Flax's directive that Martin report to him for the payload while Schriever could follow funding. Martin rejected Evans' procedural draft, so the dual management structure stayed, and the question was shelved until Phase II. It then describes MOL black and white financial procedures (4 Nov and Dec 1965 agreements), the creation and reorganization of the MOL Systems Office under Program Directive 65-1, and the first MOL Program Review Conference, which approved deviations from acquisition regulations.

nodes.title: mol finanCial proCedureS
nodes.summary: Describes MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) organization and finances. Covers the 1965 management limbo until Phase II; the 'black' MOL financial agreement of 4 Nov 1965 between Flax and Schriever (joint NRO/MOL cost estimates, fund obligation via Director of Special Projects); the December 1965 'white' funds agreement via AFSC/SSD; the MOL Systems Office creation under Program Directive 65-1; the reorganized SPO structure effective 1 Oct 1965; and the September 1965 review conference on applying AFR 375 regulations and Aerospace Corporation's GSE/TD support.

nodes.title: the mol SyStemS offiCe
nodes.summary: Chapter IX covers the organization of MOL contract definition. It describes the late-1965 management limbo, the 1965 'black' MOL financial procedures (NRO Comptroller proposal, the 4 November agreement between Flax and Schriever, and cost-estimate and obligation responsibilities), and the December 'white' financial agreement routed through AFSC/SSD. It also covers the MOL Systems Office: Program Directive 65-1, the SPO's reorganization effective 1 October, the September 1965 Program Review Conference, and Aerospace Corporation's MOL Systems Engineering Office.

nodes.title: the ContraCtor team
nodes.summary: Describes the 1965 MOL decision to select two contractors, Douglas Aircraft and General Electric, over the original single-contractor plan. It covers the 60-day study awards, the June 1965 rationale for integrating the two strongest firms, and the July 1965 division of work into laboratory vehicle, sensor module, and sensor package tasks. It also notes Zuckert's August endorsement, which cited each firm's strengths and test facilities, and McNamara's and the President's approval.

nodes.title: initiating ContraCt definition
nodes.summary: Describes MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) contract definition in 1965-66: the Titan III booster was the only segment with a Phase I contract; RFPs went to Douglas (laboratory vehicle) and General Electric (mission module); the SPO issued a program management plan. Cost breakdowns ($62M approved) and funding releases followed. Douglas signed a $10.55M fixed-price contract, GE a $4.922M contract, and Douglas selected subcontractors (Hamilton-Standard, Collins Radio, Honeywell, Pratt & Whitney). The Air Force rejected Douglas's IBM data management award over Univac, and Schriever advised avoiding congressional criticism in subcontracting. Endnotes list sources.

summary: Organization of the 1965 MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) contract definition: a dispute between Schriever and Martin led to two management channels approved by McNamara, with roles for Berg, Martin's Sensor Payload Office, and Evans, plus leadership changes at NRO, the Air Force and DDR&E. It covers the 'black' and 'white' financial agreements, the MOL Systems Office under Program Directive 65-1, and the selection of Douglas and General Electric as contractors. It also covers Phase I/II contract initiation, Titan III, the fixed-price contracts, and subcontractor and data-management award issues.

title: the manned/unmanned SyStem StudieS 1965 - 1966

nodes.title: the manned/unmanned SyStem StudieS 1965 - 1966 (intro)
nodes.summary: Covers the 1965-66 MOL unmanned-system debate. Contract work began as officials studied a wholly unmanned system that some feared would end the manned MOL. Edwin Land (PSAC) challenged USAF claims that unmanned operation would lose resolution and delay the schedule, and recommended a fully automatic camera payload that could fly with or without a man. USAF argued manned operation would give better than 1-foot resolution more reliably. Hornig and Brown agreed to develop a manned or unmanned 1-foot capability, with an unmanned demo nine months after the first manned flight. McMillan ordered manned/unmanned analyses and an automatic-subsystem study. Officers wanted the design optimized for manned operation, but Brown committed to a common optical system. Schriever and Flax said the sensor would be optimized for man-in-the-loop and then automated. PSAC reemphasized the unmanned option at a November 1965 meeting with MOL personnel, Kodak, and the Bureau of the Budget.

nodes.title: pSaC reemphaSizeS the u nmanned SyStem
nodes.summary: Describes 1965-1966 Air Force and NRO deliberations on the Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL) manned versus unmanned configurations. Covers the Hornig-Brown agreement for a better-than-1-foot resolution system with an unmanned flight nine months after the first manned flight; McMillan's directive for analyses; PSAC Reconnaissance Panel meetings and its push for a single dual-mode design; Schriever's and Flax's responses; mid-December studies finding automation feasible with unmanned resolution approaching manned; Berg's contract changes and schedule slips tied to Eastman Kodak optics; briefings to the panel; selection of Flight No. 6 as the first unmanned mission; and Schriever's proposal for an operational analysis of manned versus unmanned reconnaissance.

nodes.title: the role of m an in the mol
nodes.summary: Covers the MOL manned vs. unmanned debate in 1966: the panel's praise of unmanned briefings (Flight No. 6 selected), Schriever's concern over eliminating the manned version and his request for operational comparison, and the Jan 1966 directive creating Col Norman's study group on man's role, which concluded the case for a manned crew was as strong or stronger. Also covers the Budget Bureau's (Schultze) 1966 call to reexamine costs, McNamara's reply favoring dual development, and DDP&E's April 1966 study requirements comparing unmanned and manned reconnaissance performance, cost, risk, and coverage.

nodes.title: the Budget Bureau aSKS a reexamination of mol
nodes.summary: Covers 1965-1966 studies comparing manned and unmanned MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) reconnaissance systems for achieving better-than-one-foot resolution. Topics include an Air Force study group's view that retaining man lowers risk and cost; Budget Bureau (Schultze) and McNamara correspondence seeking reexamination of MOL; DDP&E directives for unmanned DORIAN alternatives and contractor studies (Lockheed, General Electric); Schriever's requests for supporting studies; NRO analysis finding manned systems photograph 15-45% more targets; Brown's final report on development costs ($1.818B manned vs. $1.50B unmanned), cloud avoidance, orbit flexibility, and scientific uses; and the August 1966 PSAC Reconnaissance Panel briefing, where panel members accepted weather-avoidance benefits but questioned claims about target verification and active-indicator detection.

nodes.title: the reConnaiSSanCe panel Briefing, auguSt 1966
nodes.summary: Describes the MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) reconnaissance debate of 1965-66. Covers claimed advantages of a crew: better target selection (about three times more high-value photos in simulations), avoiding cloud-obscured targets, choosing viewing angles, swapping special film, and orbit changes for finer resolution and daily reports. Also covers non-reconnaissance uses such as scientific experiments. The PSAC Reconnaissance Panel briefing of August 1966 is summarized: it accepted automation and an unmanned backup, doubted the simulations and the 5-inch scope, and Dr. Steininger said the panel wanted to "release man to do his job."

nodes.title: general SChriever’S farewell remarKS
nodes.summary: Covers General Schriever's 1966 retirement as AFSC head and MOL Program Director, his conviction that manned military space missions are indispensable, and his concern that Air Force pace was conservative. Also covers Gen Ferguson's succession, McNamara's Sept 1966 decision to proceed with the manned MOL at optimum pace for better-than-one-foot resolution, and the chapter's endnotes citing 1965-66 manned/unmanned study memos, PSAC comments, and BOB/McNamara correspondence.

summary: Covers 1965-66 MOL manned vs. unmanned debate: Land's push for automatic camera; USAF claims on manned resolution; Hornig-Brown 1-foot capability plan; PSAC reconnaissance panel favoring unmanned option and Flight No. 6; Col Norman study finding manned crew case as strong; Budget Bureau reexamination, costs ($1.818B manned vs $1.50B unmanned), NRO photo-yield findings; August 1966 panel briefing; Schriever's farewell and McNamara's Sept 1966 decision to proceed with manned MOL.

title: Budget, developmental, and SChedule

nodes.title: proBlemS—1965-1966
proBlemS—1965-1966 (intro)
nodes.summary: Covers MOL program budget and schedule problems in 1965-1966. OSD (Fink, Flax) cut the Air Force's FY1967 MOL request from $395M to about $374M, then McNamara limited FY1967 funding to $150M. Brown warned that schedule slips would delay the first manned flight, citing $294M and $230M alternatives. Fink backed $230M. Marks said restoring funds was unlikely. The $150M figure went into the January 1966 budget. Berg's plan assumed $237M plus carryover. Footnote notes Vietnam War costs strained defense projects.

nodes.title: SenSor development Slippage
nodes.summary: Covers the 1965-66 MOL DORIAN sensor schedule slippage: Eastman Kodak's December 1965 letter requesting a 10-month delay to first manned launch (mid-1970 risk); management reviews, Schriever and Berg reactions; Special Projects' Rochester review comparing 19-33 month unmanned development times; Flax's compressed schedules (Plans B and C); facilities construction approval; a further two-month slip and a six-month gap pushing launch to April 1970; congressional testimony on the earlier 1968-69 launch promises; and General Evans' concern about funding and contractor cost reduction.

nodes.title: the fy 1967 Budget review
nodes.summary: Describes the MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) FY1967 budget review in 1965-66: Air Force task forces and Senior Cost Review Boards analyzed contractor Phase II costs; Eastman Kodak and GE estimates were delayed, so DORIAN cost data were preliminary. The MOL Policy Committee weighed six options (program costs $1.714-2.6B) and sought an early 1969 manned flight. Schriever and Flax visited Eastman Kodak, explaining its schedule constraints and conservative staffing, and agreed on a December 1969 manned flight. On 20 May 1966 the Committee adopted the seven-flight Option 6 at $1.75B, with a firm baseline to follow contractor negotiations.

nodes.title: initiating mol engineering development
initiating mol engineering development (intro)
nodes.summary: Chapter XI covers MOL funding and scheduling in 1966. Option 6 led to Phase IC contract extensions and $60M in FY66 funds, about $108M spent on definition studies. Air Force sought $230M for 1967; OSD provided $178M, and Congress added $50M for $228.4M total. The MOL Director proposed a schedule-flexible approach. Secretary Brown authorized lead-time protection spending up to $208M in 1967 until January 1967. Pre-contract cost letters were issued to Douglas, GE, and McDonnell, and 1 September 1966 became the official engineering development start.

nodes.title: endnoteS
nodes.summary: Endnotes 17-38 list Air Force MOL/DORIAN memos, messages, and meeting minutes (1965-1966) on funding, scheduling, cost reviews, and program authorization. Chapter XII covers Congressional oversight of MOL: Air Force officials prepared for hearings, DORIAN briefings were given to committee staff, and Congressman George Miller pushed for open hearings. Negotiations with Miller and Secretary Brown set hearing scope (seven areas), and a January 1966 hearing date was then rescheduled to February amid unwanted White House publicity.

nodes.title: the florida upriSing
nodes.summary: Describes the Florida media uproar over the Air Force's Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL) after President Johnson's Jan 1966 report to Congress revealed West Coast (Western Test Range) launches and a $154M Titan IIIC dual pad at the Cape. The Orlando Sentinel alleged costly duplication, prompting Senator Anderson to hold a special MOL hearing. At the Feb 7 House Space Committee session, Chairman Miller and Rep. Gurney dismissed duplication concerns, and NASA's Dr. Seamans endorsed MOL. Gurney questioned why DoD could not launch polar orbits from the Eastern Range as NASA does.

Covers 1966 MOL engineering development: Option 6 Phase IC extensions, $60M FY66 funds, ~$108M definition studies, FY67 funding ($230M sought, $178M OSD, $228.4M total with Congress's $50M add), a schedule-flexible approach, lead-time spending up to $208M, pre-contract letters to Douglas, GE, McDonnell, and 1 Sept 1966 as official start. Endnotes list 1965-66 memos on funding and scheduling. Congressional oversight: hearing preparation, DORIAN briefings, Miller's push for open hearings, seven-area scope, and a rescheduled Feb hearing. Florida media uproar over West Coast launches and a $154M Cape dual pad, duplication allegations, and Feb 7 House hearing where Miller and Gurney dismissed concerns and NASA endorsed MOL.

nodes.title: the florida u priSing
nodes.summary: Covers the early 1966 Congressional handling of the Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL). Air Force Secretary and Rep. Miller agree hearings will cover seven areas (booster, life support, tracking, ships, recovery, schedules, rendezvous). Schriever and Flax to testify. A January 1966 presidential report sparked Florida outrage over alleged duplication of facilities, including Vandenberg polar launches, prompting Sen. Anderson's special session. House hearings on 7-8 February feature NASA's Seamans and Gurney's questioning of polar launches from the Cape; Schriever defends MOL's military mission. Miller concludes no major duplication with NASA's Apollo Applications and backs Vandenberg.

nodes.title: Senator holland requeStS a meeting
nodes.summary: Covers early-1966 congressional and Air Force controversy over launching the Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL) from Vandenberg instead of Cape Kennedy. Topics: Florida delegation (Sen. Holland, Congressmen Gurney and others) pressing for hearings; a 24 February Senate committee hearing; Gehrig and Col. McGarry preparing Air Force answers; Gen. Berg's assessment of ETR launch problems (dog-leg maneuver, payload loss, risks); the 15 February meeting where Dr. Flax withheld MOL's classified mission; mass letter campaigns; President Johnson's reply defending polar launches; and an Air Force ad hoc task group finding Cape facilities cheaper but WTR more economical long-term.

nodes.title: the Senate SpaCe Committee hearingS
nodes.summary: Covers the February 24, 1966 Senate Aeronautics and Space Sciences Committee 'secret' hearings on the Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL). Dr. Foster (DoD) defended the polar orbit requirement and ruled out ETR land overflight; Senator Holland challenged the need for polar orbits, and Senator Cannon came to Foster's aid. Dr. Flax and Dr. Seamans (NASA) backed Western Test Range launches. Florida politicians' criticism of moving MOL to California faded by spring 1966, and the chapter's endnotes cite the supporting documents.

Covers 1965-66 MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) budget and schedule problems: OSD cut FY1967 funding from $395M to about $374M, then to $150M; Brown and Fink weighed $294M, $230M and $237M alternatives; Eastman Kodak's DORIAN sensor delay pushed first manned launch to April 1970. FY1967 budget review set a seven-flight Option 6 at $1.75B (May 1966), with engineering development starting 1 Sept 1966. Congressional fights followed: Florida protests over Vandenberg polar launches, February 1966 hearings with NASA support, Holland's meeting requests, and the 24 February Senate closed hearing where Foster defended polar orbit.

summary: Covers the 1965-1966 Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL) budget and schedule problems. OSD cut FY1967 funding from $395M to about $374M, then $150M; alternatives of $294M, $230M and $237M were weighed. Kodak's DORIAN sensor delay pushed the first manned launch to April 1970. A seven-flight Option 6 was set at $1.75B, with engineering development from 1 Sept 1966. Congressional fights included Florida protests over Vandenberg polar launches and a closed Senate hearing where Foster defended polar orbit.

title: air forCe/naSa Coordination

nodes.title: naSa’S gemini and the gemini B ContraCt
nodes.summary: Describes coordination between NASA and the Air Force on manned space programs in 1964-1966 amid MOL and Gemini work. Covers NASA's Gemini program and McDonnell's Gemini contracts, the Gemini B procurement dispute over management responsibility, and the 1965 Seamans-Brown and Mueller-Evans negotiations. Explains the 21 April 1966 agreement assigning NASA refurbishment of Gemini spacecraft and the Air Force Gemini B acquisition. Also covers the turnover of NASA Gemini equipment to the Air Force, and notable Gemini flights of 1965.

nodes.title: turnover of naSa equipment
nodes.summary: Covers Air Force/NASA coordination for the Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL) and Gemini B. In April 1966 the two agencies agreed NASA would refurbish Gemini spacecraft for MOL tests while the Air Force handled Gemini B acquisition; the agreement was signed 21 April 1966, and the Air Force contracted McDonnell for a $6.784 million Gemini B engineering definition study. The text then describes NASA's equipment turnover to the Air Force, including disputes over a $5 million simulator charge (later waived), and an estimated $50 million in hardware transferred by end-1966. It also covers DoD Program 631A military experiments flown on Gemini (1965-1966), the public information controversy after Gemini 5, and the Soviet reconnaissance accusations.

nodes.title: dod/naSa gemini experimentS
nodes.summary: Describes NASA/Air Force coordination on Gemini: transfer of Gemini hardware to the MOL program (about $50M by 1966); the end of USAF Program 631A with Gemini 12's splashdown in Nov 1966; its origins in the 1963 McNamara-Webb agreement and Gemini Program Planning Board; the $16.1M experiment funding and management by AFSC Detachment 2 at Houston; the public information dispute over classified photographic experiments on Gemini 5 and the resulting Soviet accusations and withdrawal of D-6; and the outcomes of experiments D-1 through D-16, most successful, some incomplete.

nodes.title: the manned SpaCe flight Committee
nodes.summary: Describes the 1965-1966 DoD/NASA effort to coordinate manned space flight. Seamans proposed joint policy-level planning; Foster agreed to meet. A proposed six-man informal committee was opposed by Schriever, who wanted to keep negotiating with Mueller, but Secretary Brown supported it. This led to the Manned Space Flight Policy Committee, superseding the Gemini Program Planning Board, signed January 1966 by McNamara, Webb, Seamans, and Foster, with Seamans and Foster as co-chairs.

nodes.title: the reConStituted naSa experimentS Board
nodes.summary: Chapter XIII on Air Force/NASA coordination. In January 1966 NASA's Manned Space Flight Experiments Board (MSFEB) was reconstituted to add DoD membership; on 21 March 1966 Seamans and Foster signed the agreement charging it with approving experiments, assigning them to flights, setting priorities, and reviewing status. Members and alternates are named. Sponsoring agencies must vet experiments first. DoD experiments for Apollo (radiation, autonomous navigation, CO2 reduction) were accepted for AS-207/209. NASA's Apollo Applications Program was outlined, including an S-IVB spent-stage shirt-sleeve workshop experiment slated for SA-209 in late 1967. The Air Force sought MOL-oriented experiments aboard it, and an ad hoc group under Yarymovych was formed to study them in April 1966.

nodes.title: dod experimentS for the apollo worKShop
nodes.summary: Covers the reconstituted NASA Manned Space Flight Experiments Board (MSFEB), which added DoD membership after a January 1966 meeting, and its formal agreement signed 21 March 1966 with its DoD and NASA members and alternates. It describes the review process before experiments go to the Board. It then traces DoD experiments for Apollo: three earlier Air Force experiments (Radiation, Autonomous Navigation, CO2 Reduction) assigned to AS-207 and AS-209. It covers NASA's post-Apollo Applications Program and the S-IVB spent stage workshop concept, which led the Air Force to plan MOL-oriented workshop experiments. An ad hoc group selected six experiments, five of which were approved in September 1966 and contracted. The text covers the NASA workshop launch plan shifting toward a rendezvous mode, Air Force schedule concerns, Mueller's reassurances, the expanded four-launch plan, the November 1966 Board approvals, and the eight experiments scheduled for flight by year-end 1966.

nodes.title: aap uSe of titan iii/mol h ardware
nodes.summary: Chapter XIII covers 1966–1967 coordination between NASA and the Air Force over the Titan III/MOL hardware. The Bureau of the Budget sought alternatives to cut costs, and a House subcommittee criticized AAP/MOL duplication. DDR&E ordered a MOL Systems Office study, which found MOL/Titan III could support AAP experiments with modifications. NASA's November 1966 report opposing MOL use was rejected by DoD (General Evans and Dr. Foster) as biased and not joint. PSAC's post-Apollo report urged MOL use for biomedical studies, and McNamara proposed a joint DoD/NASA study in 1967. Endnotes list the supporting source documents.

summary: Covers 1964-1967 Air Force/NASA coordination on manned spaceflight. Topics: NASA's Gemini program and the Gemini B contract dispute, the 21 April 1966 agreement (NASA refurbishes Gemini for MOL, Air Force acquires Gemini B), equipment turnover (~$50M by end-1966, $5M simulator charge waived), DoD Program 631A Gemini experiments and their end, the Gemini 5 public information dispute and Soviet accusations, and the Manned Space Flight Policy Committee. Also covers the reconstituted MSFEB with DoD membership (March 1966), DoD experiments for Apollo and the Apollo Applications Program workshop, and the Titan III/MOL hardware dispute with cost criticism, NASA's opposition, PSAC's biomedical recommendation, and a proposed joint study.

title: new finanCial and SChedule proBlemS 1967-1968

nodes.title: the fy 1968 Budget CriSiS
nodes.summary: Covers MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) program developments in 1967-1968: its Phase II engineering start in September 1966, Air Force urgency, and contract cost disputes resolved by a tough negotiating stance, yielding about $1.92 billion in development costs. The FY1968 budget crisis followed as OSD cut NOA to $430 million, prompting schedule slip debates (12 vs. 15 months), funding limits of $480 million for FY1968, and the decision on a 'compact 12' schedule targeting a December 1970 manned flight. Also covers contract awards to McDonnell-Douglas, General Electric, management reform, rising costs ($2.35 billion), and preparations for McNamara's secret visit to Eastman Kodak.

nodes.title: mcn amara viSitS eaStman KodaK
nodes.summary: Covers 1967 MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) program funding and schedule problems. Officials reviewed a pessimistic report and agreed on a $480 million FY1968 budget, leading to a 12-month 'compact' schedule targeting a December 1970 first manned flight. Phase II contracts were awarded to McDonnell Douglas ($855M total) and General Electric ($110M). Concerns grew over Vietnam War budget cuts. McNamara visited Eastman Kodak in September 1967 after a report on high-resolution DORIAN photography. Congress allotted only $430 million, creating a $50 million shortfall, which forced a further 12-week slip to 1971. A third schedule revision in December 1967 proposed an August 1971 launch, endorsed by contractors and a review council.

nodes.title: the third maJ or SChedule reviSion of 1967
nodes.summary: Covers the MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) program in 1967-1968: photo-resolution comparisons (KH-8, KH-7, DORIAN/MOL) favoring MOL; McNamara's September 1967 Eastman Kodak visit; a $40-50 million funding shortfall, Congress allotting only $430 million, and a 12-week schedule slip to 1971; the December 1967 contractor-revised schedule (first manned launch August 1971, $661 million FY69 assumption); McNamara's $400 million challenge and Brown's reply recommending $600 million (or $520 million with stretchout); events of 1968 (Pueblo seizure, Tet offensive, political assassinations) affecting budgets; and termination-cost estimates of $46.7 million, with the Budget Director saying reprogramming could cover costs.

nodes.title: Cia and State department oppoSition
nodes.summary: In early 1968, opposition grew to MOL. On 14 February, Ambassador Bohlen questioned whether the $2.4 billion program was worth it, noting about $722 million spent and proposing a study; Dr. Foster replied that the program had been reviewed and endorsed by senior officials, and offered a Defense Department briefing. CIA Director Helms expressed reservations on 5 March about resolution better than one foot and began a review, completed by mid-May. The CIA found very high resolution would aid intelligence on Soviet and Chinese weapons, but concluded it would not significantly change key estimates, and that the pivotal question was whether the added value justified the cost.

nodes.title: trouBle on the CongreSSional front
nodes.summary: Covers 1968 congressional and budget struggles of the MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) program. The CIA and Bureau of the Budget opposed it; a March 1968 NRO briefing to Chairman Mahon showed GAMBIT 3 resolution, and Foster and Flax defended MOL's need. Mahon asked whether they favored MOL; both said yes. CIA's Duckett noted Helms's reservations about cost. Defense budget cuts, the $6B surtax-related reduction, and a Congressional Quarterly critique targeting MOL followed. General Stewart met Senate staffer Woodruff, warning of viability thresholds. Congress appropriated $515M for FY1969, forcing schedule slips to December 1971. Air Force hoped for Nixon's support. Includes endnote citations.

summary: Covers MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) funding and schedule crises in 1967-1968: Phase II contracts (McDonnell Douglas, GE), cost growth to $2.35B, Congress cutting NOA to $430M, schedule slips (12 to 15 weeks, then to 1971), McNamara's Eastman Kodak visit, CIA/State opposition over resolution and cost, and congressional fights including $515M FY1969 appropriation, termination-cost estimates, and efforts to win White House support.

title: the proJeCt terminated

nodes.title: the proJeCt terminated (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes the MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) project's late-1968 to early-1969 review. A DDR&E ad hoc group's Development Concept Paper defended very high resolution photography against CIA objections and offered three funding options. Foster, Nitze, Hornig and the OSD Comptroller backed a $575M FY70 baseline, while CIA Director Helms dissented. The paper and companion documents went to the incoming Laird/Packard team. A new secondary mission was approved before the Nixon inauguration. In February 1969 Packard received a favorable Stewart briefing, but BOB's Mayo questioned MOL's value against the GAMBIT-3 satellite. CSD officials rebutted that critique.

nodes.title: the fight to Save the program
nodes.summary: Covers the 1969 fight to save the Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL). Laird trimmed the defense budget and dropped unmanned vehicles, and OSD/BOB reviewed MOL alternatives with cost estimates. Packard approved a four-manned-vehicle program at $556 million for FY1970 on 6 March 1969. Congressional and press criticism of the military-industrial complex, including Benson's article and Brademas's Congressional Record insertion, grew. Briefings to Congress on MOL's resolution met skepticism, and Mansfield named MOL an economy target. The Budget Bureau demanded termination, and Mayo took the issue to the President with alternative funding options and a draft issue paper.

nodes.title: mayo taKeS the mol iSSue to the preSident
nodes.summary: Covers 1969 internal debate over the Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL). Senate briefings showed MOL's high-resolution photography, but a staffer doubted its persuasiveness. Congress, led by Senate Majority Leader Mansfield, targeted defense cuts, listing MOL as an economy target. The Budget Bureau pushed termination, arguing GAMBIT-3 was nearly as good. OSD rebutted, citing photographic accuracy and arms-control verification value. Laird cut MOL's budget to $525 million. The President then cut FY1970 funding to $360 million and terminated HEXAGON. Stewart outlined schedule delays and cost options, including continuing only the camera for unmanned use. Officials considered merging DORIAN and HEXAGON, and drafted memos to the President. Mayo urged termination, citing MOL's high per-mission cost (about $150 million versus $23 million for GAMBIT-3) and questionable added value.

nodes.title: the white houSe meeting of 17 may 1969
nodes.summary: Covers the May 1969 White House meeting and the termination of the NRO's Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL). It describes Aviation Week reports of budget threats, Seamans' Senate testimony, and a 9 May MOL Policy Committee review where Bleymaier requested funding. It then details the 17 May briefing to President Nixon by Seamans and Stewart, Nixon's decision to cancel MOL in favor of HEXAGON, his Air Force Academy speech, and Packard's 9 June termination directive with close-out funding. Also covered: congressional notification, Laird's justification, Senator Cannon's and McIntyre's criticisms, endnotes, and the post-cancellation impact on personnel, including layoffs and a letter from a affected employee's daughter.

summary: Describes the late-1968 to 1969 review of the Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL): DDR&E's Development Concept Paper defended high-resolution photography against CIA objections, and the incoming Laird/Packard team received it. Packard approved a $556M FY1970 program, but congressional and Budget Bureau pressure and GAMBIT-3 comparisons mounted. Mayo took the issue to the President, who cut funding and terminated HEXAGON. At the 17 May 1969 White House meeting Nixon canceled MOL in favor of HEXAGON; Packard's 9 June directive followed, with layoffs and congressional criticism.

title: poSt-mortem

nodes.title: mol program CoStS
nodes.summary: Post-mortem of the cancelled MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) program in June-September 1969. Contractors McDonnell Douglas, General Electric, Eastman Kodak and the Titan IIIM group halted work and cut personnel sharply (e.g., McDonnell Douglas 6,263 to 369). Eight MOL astronauts were reassigned to NASA. Program costs reached about $1.54 billion, with $125 million requested for termination costs, reduced to $128 million in claims. Hardware disposition studies for reuse by USAF or NASA followed.

nodes.title: h ardware diSpoSition
nodes.summary: Describes the wind-down of the MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) program: termination costs rose to about $1.54 billion, and the FY1970 line item was cut from $525M to $125.3M to cover severance, settlements, and disposition. Hardware disposition was studied by an ad hoc group chaired by Dr. Yarymovych, which recommended transfers of unclassified and classified equipment to NASA, AFOSR, the Western Test Range, Air Force labs, and the Avionics Laboratory. NASA also expressed interest in GE and Eastman Kodak technology, leading to study contracts. The MOL Program Office closed on 15 February 1970, and the Systems Office was slated to close 30 June 1970.

nodes.title: Could the program have Been Saved?
nodes.summary: Covers the post-mortem on the cancelled Manned Orbiting Laboratory (MOL): whether it could have been saved by flying the man-rated system alone (decoupling optics, per General Evans' March 1966 suggestion) and General Momyer's 1964 concern about putting all man-in-space eggs in the reconnaissance basket. It explains MOL lost out to Vietnam War budget pressures and CIA/BOB arguments favoring unmanned reconnaissance, traces Air Force space flight ambitions from 1945 through Dyna-Soar, and notes the shift toward a NASA space shuttle. Also includes Senator Russell's 1969 remarks and endnote sources.

summary: Post-mortem of the cancelled MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) program, 1969-1970: contractor work halts and layoffs, eight astronauts reassigned to NASA, costs of about $1.54B and termination claims, and hardware disposition to NASA and USAF (Yarymovych group, office closures). Also asks whether MOL could have been saved (decoupling optics, Momyer's 1964 concern, Vietnam budget pressure, CIA/BOB favoring unmanned reconnaissance), Air Force space ambitions from 1945 through Dyna-Soar, and the shift toward the NASA shuttle.

title: Supplemental doCumentS index
summary: An index of supplemental documents from the 2015 compendium "The DORIAN Files Revealed: A Compendium of the NRO's Manned Orbiting Laboratory Documents" (August 2015). It lists roughly 1,200 numbered MOL (Manned Orbiting Laboratory) documents from 1962 to 1971 plus 1976 and 1978, with each entry's title, date, and page count. Topics include program authorization, management and security, contractors and source selection, public affairs and foreign policy, the DORIAN camera system, the termination in 1969, and residual hardware transfers to NASA.
